relations.definition: The source concept is a constituent, phase, or subtopic of the target concept.
positive_examples: LoRA is part of parameter-efficient fine-tuning.
Latency is part of serving evaluation.
negative_examples: A appears near B without a part-whole statement.

relations.definition: The source requires the target as a prerequisite, input, or enabling condition.
negative_examples: A merely uses B as one optional tool.
A only appears after B in a list.

relations.definition: The output or result of the source becomes an input to the target.
positive_examples: Evaluation results feed into model selection.
negative_examples: Two ideas are compared side by side.
A constrains B without producing an input.

relations.definition: The source and target are explicitly contrasted, benchmarked, or considered as alternatives.
positive_examples: Offline evaluation compares with online evaluation.

relations.definition: The source limits, governs, or narrows how the target can be used.
The source is stated to increase, improve, reduce cost of, or otherwise benefit the target.
The source risk threatens, degrades, or can harm the target.
negative_examples: A is a metric for B.

relations.definition: The source measures, judges, validates, or scores the target.
The source invokes the target service, control, or external dependency.
positive_examples: The orchestrator calls the model server.
The application calls a tool service.
negative_examples: A reads persisted data from B.
A is a prerequisite for B.

relations.definition: The source chooses, forwards, or dispatches work to the target.
positive_examples: A router routes requests to a model endpoint.
A gateway routes traffic to the application.

relations.definition: The source reads existing data from the target datastore.
positive_examples: The retriever reads from a vector store.
negative_examples: A writes new records to B.
A sends a network request to B.

relations.definition: The source writes new or updated data to the target datastore.
positive_examples: The ingestion pipeline writes embeddings to the vector store.
The monitor writes events to logs.

relations.definition: The source stores artifacts or state in the target datastore.
positive_examples: The application stores conversation state in a database.
The pipeline stores chunks in a document store.
negative_examples: A depends on B as a concept.

relations.definition: The source consumes, invokes, or relies on the target at runtime without asserting prerequisite semantics.
negative_examples: A is strictly required before B can function.
A feeds its output into B.

relations.definition: The source observes, logs, traces, or measures the target.
negative_examples: A calls B to complete user work.

relations.definition: The source sends requests, messages, events, or data to the target.
positive_examples: The client sends a prompt to the application.
The retriever sends context to the generator.
negative_examples: A only labels B as risky.

relations.definition: An architecture node realizes a concept, method, or control directly.
negative_examples: An architecture node merely stores data for a concept.

relations.definition: The source enables the target without directly realizing it.
negative_examples: The source directly implements the target.
The source and target are both in a same-layer relation.

relations.definition: A concept, control, or decision governs or is relevant to a specific architecture node or stage.
positive_examples: Latency applies to the model server.
Guardrails apply to the application service.
